title: Neuromodulators as precision weighting machinery
excerpt: The precision matrices in the hierarchical free-energy decomposition act as multiplicative gain fields over prediction-error units: they amplify mismatches deemed reliable and suppress those attributable to noise. Implementing this operation requires mechanism
html:
The precision matrices Πl\Pi_l in the hierarchical free-energy decomposition act as multiplicative gain fields over prediction-error units: they amplify mismatches deemed reliable and suppress those attributable to noise. Implementing this operation requires mechanisms that can multiplicatively rescale neural input-output functions in a context-dependent, rapidly adjustable manner. The ascending neuromodulatory systems–acetylcholine (ACh), norepinephrine (NE), dopamine (DA), and serotonin (5-HT)–are natural candidates, sharing three properties that distinguish them from fast synaptic transmission and that map directly onto precision-weighting requirements 1, 2: (i) broad but topographically organized projections from compact source nuclei, enabling a single modulatory signal to set different effective precisions across areas via area- and layer-specific receptor distributions; (ii) slow, often metabotropic signaling (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds) that modulates on the timescale of contextual state–arousal, volatility, attentional set–rather than individual spikes; and (iii) multiplicative (gain-like) effects on neuronal input-output functions, achieved through modulation of leak conductances (e.g., ACh (via muscarinic receptors) often suppresses M-type (Kv7) K+ currents, increasing input resistance and excitability, while NE often modulates neuronal gain through receptor-specific effects on intrinsic conductances and inhibitory circuitry that can either enhance or suppress excitability), suppression of spike-frequency adaptation (extending linear dynamic range), alteration of synaptic conductance states (shifting normalization set points), and modulation of dendritic Ca2+ and NMDA nonlinearities that gate compartment-specific regenerative events 3.

The theoretical link to predictive coding was made explicit by Friston: in the cortical hierarchy, superficial pyramidal neurons encoding prediction error εl\varepsilon_l have their postsynaptic gain set by neuromodulatory input; a neuromodulator that multiplicatively increases this gain is, formally, increasing the precision Πl\Pi_l–causing the same physical mismatch to exert greater influence on both perceptual inference and synaptic learning 4, 5. Conversely, reducing gain on error units is equivalent to declaring those errors unreliable, allowing other synapses/neurons to dominate. This framing unifies classical observations of neuromodulatory sensory enhancement with Bayesian inference: "turning up the volume" on a sensory area is increasing sensory likelihood precision relative to prior expectations. Each neuromodulator controls a distinct axis of the precision landscape:

ACh – sensory likelihood precision. Yu and Dayan formalized ACh as signaling expected uncertainty–the known unreliability of top-down predictions–boosting the weight of bottom-up evidence relative to descending priors 1. Mechanistically, β2\beta2 nicotinic receptors (often α4β2\alpha4\beta2-containing) expressed on thalamocortical afferents in granular layers (e.g., L4) potentiate feedforward drive, while muscarinic receptors (via subtype- and circuit-specific mechanisms, often involving presynaptic modulation and inhibitory interneurons) suppress intracortical recurrent and feedback transmission that carries lateral and top-down predictions 6, 7–a coordinated shift that raises sensory precision and lowers prior precision. Empirically, sustained attention elevates cortical ACh and improves detection 8; optogenetic basal-forebrain ACh activation enhances visual cortical gain and perceptual sensitivity 9; cholinesterase inhibition enhances the mismatch negativity (MMN), with dynamic causal modeling localizing the effect to increased gain on forward prediction-error connections 10. Cholinergic tone also controls cortical state: high ACh decorrelates population activity, reducing shared variability and increasing effective coding precision 11; low ACh (non-REM sleep) allows synchronized, prior-dominated dynamics suited to consolidation rather than inference. See the "Acetylcholine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these ACh functions through architectural biases and specific training data.

NE – volatility and global gain reset. NE from the locus coeruleus (LC) encodes unexpected uncertainty (volatility)–the degree to which the generative model itself has become unreliable 1, 12. Phasic LC bursts deliver a transient, brain-wide precision boost that amplifies whichever prediction errors are currently active, forcing rapid belief updating (consistent with the P3/P300 scalp potential scaling with surprise 13). Tonic LC mode sets baseline gain and the exploitation-exploration trade-off: intermediate tonic NE sharpens gain selectively on task-relevant representations (exploitation); high tonic NE elevates gain uniformly, washing out differential precision and promoting disengagement and exploration 12. At the cellular level, moderate NE engages high-affinity α2A\alpha2A receptors, strengthening prefrontal recurrent dynamics (e.g., via inhibition of cAMP signaling and closure of HCN channels on spines), whereas high NE release during stress recruits lower-affinity α1\alpha1 and β1\beta1 receptors that weaken PFC network persistence and impair working memory–yielding the classic inverted-U dose-response for prefrontal function 14, 15, 16. See the "Norepinephrine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these NE functions through architectural biases and specific training data.

DA – prior/policy precision. Mesocortical DA modulates the gain of prefrontal representations–the confidence assigned to abstract goals and rules maintained in working memory. Intermediate D1R stimulation stabilizes and sharpens persistent PFC representations (improved signal-to-noise/selectivity/precision) via multiple synaptic and intrinsic mechanisms, producing an inverted-U optimum 17, 18. Insufficient D1 stimulation yields imprecise priors (distractible, stimulus-bound inference); excessive D1 stimulation aberrant precision control (e.g., maladaptive weighting of priors vs prediction-errors)–a leading computational account of psychotic positive symptoms 19, 20 and THC effects 21. D2-dominated regimes reduce attractor stability and facilitate rapid switching/updating (lower ‘policy commitment’), supporting flexibility 22, 23. In active inference, the policy precision parameter γ\gamma governing the softmax over policies has been formally identified with dopaminergic signaling, linking parkinsonian akinesia to low γ\gamma and impulsivity/mania to high γ\gamma 24. See the "Dopamine" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these DA functions through architectural biases and specific training data. Precision sets the weight of beliefs and expectations. (Figure). Dopamine responses depend on how predictive the cue is. (Figure).

5-HT – temporal depth and prior-likelihood balance. Serotonin’s 14+ receptor subtypes resist a single computational gloss, but convergent evidence supports roles in modulating the temporal horizon of the loss (high 5-HT promotes patience / low discounting, effectively increasing the weight assigned to distal outcomes / long-horizon errors (a temporal-depth meta-parameter 25, 26) and the learning rate under volatility 27. High 5-HT2A expression in deep-layer pyramidal populations and (apical) dendrite-rich compartments (notably layer V/Va) in prefrontal/association cortex positions serotonin to gate the gain on top-down feedback at the dendritic level 28, 29. 5-HT-2A agonists (psychedelics) profoundly disrupt prior-likelihood balance, producing states interpretable as collapsed or chaotically fluctuating prior precision: the REBUS model (Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics) formalizes this as a flattening of the precision hierarchy, releasing sensory processing from the constraint of high-level priors 30. See the "Serotonin" section of "Neuromodulators" for a detailed account of how evolution "baked in" these 5-HT functions through architectural biases and specific training data.

Much of the cortex’s fine-grained spatial specificity in neuromodulatory gain control is achieved not only by direct action on pyramidal neurons, but also–and often more selectively–through differential recruitment of inhibitory interneuron subtypes, providing the circuit-level mechanism by which a diffuse broadcast can yield compartment- and pathway-specific gain adjustments. VIP+^+ interneurons (many within the 5-HT3_{3}-expressing interneuron class and strongly excitable by nicotinic ACh) can act as neuromodulatory relay switches: when recruited, they suppress SST+^+ dendrite-targeting inhibition (the VIP→\rightarrowSST disinhibitory motif), thereby disinhibiting pyramidal distal/apical dendrites and increasing dendritic responsiveness–an arrangement consistent with a state-dependent "opening of the gate" for signals that preferentially impinge on apical compartments (including, plausibly, feedback/contextual inputs) 31, 32. PV+^+ basket cells, by contrast, deliver fast perisomatic inhibition that strongly shapes spike output and population gain; neuromodulators that alter PV excitability and PV-driven E/I balance can therefore shift cortical responses in a manner consistent with divisive gain control/normalization, even if normalization itself is implemented by multiple interacting mechanisms 33, 32. SST+^+ neurons provide the complementary handle, targeting dendritic compartments (often distal/apical) more directly and thereby modulating apical integration itself 32. Taken together, these subtype-specific targeting rules (PV: perisomatic output control; SST: dendritic/apical inhibition; VIP: dendritic disinhibition via SST) furnish a concrete substrate by which neuromodulators can differentially reweight feedforward-dominated drive (often impacting spike output via perisomatic control) versus feedback/contextual influences (often impacting apical integration), enabling a partially dissociable tuning of effective likelihood- vs prior-related precision in hierarchical predictive coding (the dendritic mechanisms are elaborated in the next subsection).

Overall, the four neuromodulatory systems implement a multi-dimensional state space over the cortex’s precision landscape. No single neuromodulator "is" precision; each controls a different axis (sensory likelihood, volatility/global gain, prior/policy confidence, temporal depth), and these axes interact through dense inter-nuclear connectivity and receptor co-expression. The joint neuromodulatory state is coordinately reshaped across behavioral contexts–from drowsy rest (low ACh, low NE -> low sensory precision, prior-dominated) to alert focused attention (high ACh, moderate phasic NE, optimal DA -> high sensory precision, sharp policy precision) to acute stress (high tonic NE, high DA, low 5-HT -> uniformly high but poorly differentiated gain, shallow temporal horizon)–tuning the effective cortical loss function to the demands of the moment (see the "Computational Integration" section of "Neuromodulators" for more). Importantly, these gain changes do not themselves compute prediction errors; they weight them. In machine-learning terms, neuromodulators are not part of the forward pass that computes the loss but part of the optimizer–they set the effective learning rate and the relative weighting of loss terms, moment by moment, across the cortical hierarchy. Striatal dopamine tracks sensory prediction errors during preconditioning (Figure) 34. Striatal dopamine tracks value-based reward prediction errors during classical conditioning (Figure).
